Modernization of a Historical Prostate Cancer Registry using Artificial Intelligence: A Tale of Two Large Language Models.
desc: [The Journal of urology] Since 1986, the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry has followed over 30,000 patients who underwent radical prostatectomy. Advances in LLMs may modernize data collection, reduce human abstraction burden, and improve registry efficiency. Herein, we report the results of LLM data abstraction for surgical pathology and prostate MRI data in the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry. Surgical pathology and MRI reports were obtained for 3,210 and 4,739 patients, respectively, who underwent radical prostatectomy from 2010-2022. LLM prompts for 13 pathology and 20 MRI variables were developed and ran through two independent LLMs (Google Gemini Flash 1.5, 2.0, or 2.5). LLM outputs were compared to human-abstracted data. Median consensus LLM error rate for pathology report data was 0.09%(IQR 0.03-0.16%), compared with median human error rate of 2.81%(IQR 1.83-3.17%). Individual LLMs had threefold higher error rates compared to consensus LLM (LLM 1: 0.27%(IQR 0.09-0.34%), LLM 2: 0.30%(IQR 0.17%-0.48%)). For MRI reports, median consensus LLM error rate was 0.17%(IQR 0.00-0.68%), compared with human error rate of 1.01%(IQR 0.59-3.20%). Individual LLMs had error rates of 0.84%(IQR 0.34-2.79%) and 1.02%(IQR 0.34-1.67%). Estimated time for human data abstraction across all 136,510 data elements was 952 hours, compared with 32 hours for our LLM pipeline. LLM data abstraction employing a consensus vote across two independent LLMs consistently yielded higher accuracy than human or single-LLM abstraction. A dual-LLM consensus architecture may improve data abstraction efficiency, reduce errors, and should be considered for integration into all prospectively maintained longitudinal clinical registries.

title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
desc: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. In clinical practice, however, diagnosis is an iterative process of inquiry. Clinicians take the patient's history, or anamnesis (Hx), through targeted questioning, examine the patient, and request and interpret tests, progressively narrowing the differential until they reach a final diagnosis (Dx). We introduce Hx2Dx ARENA, an interactive benchmark of 1'000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). Each case is a simulated encounter that proceeds from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. We evaluate open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations. Performance varies considerably across models in the interactive setting, and every model loses diagnostic accuracy relative to the static setting, where the full case is presented upfront. The ability to ask the right questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the loss of accuracy: diagnosis improves as questions become more targeted and build a more complete clinical picture. LLMs thus reason well once the relevant data are available but remain limited in hypothesis-driven information gathering, in knowing what to ask in order to know. Closing this gap is a prerequisite for their safe integration into real-world diagnostic workflows.

title: “发挥生物·医疗健康专业优势，助力AI就业”……阿视亚经济培养医疗AI与生物融合领域专才
Artificial Intelligence‒Guided Phenotyping of Cardiomyopathies: From Detection to Surveillance.
desc: [Journal of cardiac failure] The management of cardiomyopathies relies on timely diagnosis, precise phenotyping, multimodal risk stratification, and longitudinal monitoring. These tasks require integration of high-dimensional signals from patient history, electrocardiography, imaging, biomarkers, and longitudinal health records, data streams well-suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled pattern recognition and prediction. Among inherited and acquired cardiomyopathies, hypertrophic (HCM) and transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) best exemplify this opportunity. Both remain systematically underdiagnosed, span a continuous phenotypic spectrum, and are increasingly actionable through disease-modifying therapies. Emerging AI approaches applied to multimodality data streams can identify latent disease, quantify its severity, and predict its trajectory. Beyond diagnosis, AI paves the path for opportunistic screening, longitudinal surveillance, risk stratification, and novel clinical trial designs. Realizing this promise requires careful attention to label quality, generalizability, false-positive burden in low-prevalence settings, and prospective evidence that the human-AI synergy improves outcomes. In this review, we use HCM and ATTR-CM as key examples to synthesize the current evidence of AI in cardiomyopathies and propose a forward-looking framework for AI-guided disease phenotyping, with emphasis on regulation, implementation, and clinical evaluation.

title: BioXArena-Pro: a research-grade benchmark for autonomous biomedical machine learning agents
desc: Coding agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous builders of biomedical models, but existing benchmarks are small, near saturation or open to leaked information. We present BioXArena-Pro, 64 research-level modelling tasks from eight biomedical domains, each rebuilt from a published study; most hold out whole biological units such as species or cohorts. Across 22 agent configurations, the best scores 55.1 of 100, and the scaffold matters almost as much as the model. We re-ran a published method for every task: where the published recipe applies unchanged, the best agent and the methods tie; on rebuilt tasks the methods trail by 8.2 points, suggesting that agents gain by adapting to new data. Pretrained models (including biological foundation models) matter where the strongest agent uses them: forbidding them decreases its score on those tasks by 9 points. Every task was audited in several AI-assisted rounds and a final human review.

title: 中国平安亮相世界互联网大会乌镇峰会，以AI医疗打通复杂疾病全程服务
Machine learning-driven ECG screening for early coronary artery disease detection.
desc: [Asian cardiovascular & thoracic annals] BackgroundElectrocardiography (ECG) is inexpensive and widely available, yet its ability to detect early and nonobstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) is limited when interpreted using conventional criteria. We evaluated whether a deep learning model applied to standard 12-lead-ECG images can identify angiographically confirmed CAD and enable clinically meaningful risk stratification in a real-world population.MethodsIn this multicentric study, 15,890 ECG-angiography pairs (12-lead ECG paired with coronary angiography [CA] or coronary CT angiography [CCTA]) were included between November 2021 and January 2024. A DenseNet-121 convolutional neural network was trained to predict CAD from ECG images. Temporal validation was performed on a prospectively collected, independent cohort of 2168 samples from February to May 2024. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), PR-AUC, and standard diagnostic metrics. Robustness across varying disease prevalence was evaluated using simulation, and prevalence-dependent predictive performance was summarized using PPV and NPV prevalence curves (AUCppv and AUCnpv).ResultsThe model was trained on 13,299 samples, validated on 1,002, and tested on 1339 (CAD prevalence 52.9%). On the test set, ROC-AUC was 0.80 and PR-AUC 0.83. At the optimal 0.50 threshold, sensitivity was 87% (618/708 CAD cases detected) and specificity 50% (317/631 non-CAD correctly classified). On the temporal validation set (n = 2168; 64% CAD), ROC-AUC was 0.81 and PR-AUC 0.83, with sensitivity 0.67, specificity 0.78, PPV 0.84, and NPV 0.57. Simulated prevalence analyses demonstrated robust PPV/NPV trends across distributions.ConclusionDeep learning analysis of routinely acquired ECG images can identify patients at increased risk of CAD and may support low-cost, scalable CAD risk stratification.

title: Influence of the branching geometry on SPION propagation: coupling of experiment and simulation
desc: Magnetic Drug Targeting (MDT) is an emerging therapeutic concept in cancer medicine, where superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) are used as carriers for medication. Their magnetic properties allow for the manipulation of particle transport within the vascular structure and thus targeted delivery to the tumor site. To develop effective concepts for particle steering and accumulation, a detailed understanding of the particle--flow interaction, especially at asymmetric vascular bifurcations, is needed. Based on hierarchical scaling laws, generalized bifurcation geometries with varying degrees of asymmetry were derived and additively manufactured. The particle distribution was investigated by in situ optical measurements under different flow conditions and magnetic field configurations and compared with Lagrangian particle and Volume of Fluid Simulations (VoFS). While the particle mass partition followed the hydraulic flow split in asymmetric bifurcations, density-driven stratification dominated in the symmetric bifurcation, where one daughter branch received only a minor fraction of the particle mass at low flow rates despite carrying half of the flow. The Lagrangian model reproduced the predominantly advective propagation, whereas only the VoFS approach captured the stratification-induced asymmetry. Magnetic actuation counteracted the stratification, reversed the passive branch preference and increased particle retention. From a molecular communication perspective, bifurcation geometry, collective volume effects and magnetic actuation thus jointly determine the received particle signal at vascular bifurcations.

title: Artificial intelligence in the in vitro fertilization laboratory: A scoping review and SWOT-based evaluation of emerging applications.
source: PubMed · Clinical and experimental reproductive medicine
desc: [Clinical and experimental reproductive medicine] Artificial intelligence (AI) represents a potentially transformative tool in assisted reproductive technology (ART), particularly in vitro fertilization (IVF), for gamete assessment, embryo selection, non-invasive genetic testing, and laboratory automation. This scoping review synthesized recent evidence on AI applications in IVF laboratories and evaluated their translational maturity using an evidence maturity framework and a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis. This scoping review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed studies published from January 2020 to February 2025. Eligible studies evaluated AI, machine learning, or deep learning in laboratory components of ART. Data were charted on AI methods, dataset characteristics, validation strategies, clinical endpoints, and performance metrics. Ninety-four studies were included. Most applications addressed embryo grading and implantation prediction using convolutional neural networks and were evaluated through internal cross-validation. Reported areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.75 to 0.92, depending on the endpoint and dataset size. AI applications in sperm analysis and oocyte assessment showed greater reproducibility than manual evaluation. Non-invasive genetic prediction models displayed promising but heterogeneous sensitivity and remained predominantly limited to internal validation. Few studies reported prospective evaluation or external validation using multicenter datasets. AI applications in IVF are expanding, but most remain at early stages of clinical translation. Standardized datasets, external validation, interpretable algorithms, and regulatory oversight remain necessary for safe, equitable clinical integration. AI should function as a decision-support tool that supplements, rather than replaces, embryologists' expertise.

title: DrugCoding: A Scientific Programming Agent for Drug Discovery
desc: Drug discovery involves multiple interconnected research stages, including molecular design, property prediction, and virtual screening. These processes are characterized by complex workflows, interdependent computational tasks, and diverse specialized tools, placing substantial demands on the coordination of scientific models and computational resources. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based scientific agents still face challenges in autonomous planning of complex tasks, adaptive selection of specialized models, and reliable execution of multi-stage scientific computations, limiting their effectiveness in automating complex drug discovery workflows. To address these challenges, we propose DrugCoding, a scientific programming agent system that integrates scientific task planning, adaptive model routing, multi-agent collaboration, and programmatic tool execution. DrugCoding enables autonomous task planning and dynamic model adaptation for complex research objectives. It can flexibly invoke specialized scientific models, autonomously generate and execute code according to task requirements, and leverage multi-agent collaboration to support efficient execution and reliable validation of complex scientific tasks. To evaluate DrugCoding's performance in scientific tool invocation and multi-stage task execution, we conduct multi-turn tool-calling experiments across diverse language models and scientific tool interfaces. Experimental results demonstrate that DrugCoding achieves an average session-level Pass@1 of 97.35% on the full benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline, Codex, by 9.24%. On the challenging subset, DrugCoding achieves 97.92%, exceeding the strongest baseline.

title: The evolving landscape of artificial intelligence in cholecystectomy: a bibliometric and science-mapping analysis.
desc: [Updates in surgery] To map the global research landscape and thematic evolution of artificial intelligence (AI)-related research in cholecystectomy and to identify major contributors, collaboration patterns, and intellectual foundations. English-language articles and reviews were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus. After deduplication and eligibility screening, 559 publications were included. Publication trends, scientific collaboration, keyword co-occurrence, conceptual structure, thematic evolution, and co-citation and citation-burst patterns were analyzed using bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and Python. Research activity increased markedly in recent years, with 424 publications (75.8%) appearing between 2022 and 2025. China contributed the largest publication output, whereas the United States received the highest total citations. Keyword and conceptual-structure analyses identified research domains involving AI and computational methods, surgical workflow and intraoperative visual analysis, and computer-vision-based applications. Thematic evolution suggested a progression from early workflow- and convolutional-neural-network-related research toward machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, surgical phase recognition, and more recent transformer-related approaches. Twinanda et al. [1] showed the strongest citation burst and occupied a prominent position in the reference co-citation network. AI-related research in cholecystectomy has expanded rapidly and become increasingly diverse in its methodological and application-oriented focus. Current bibliometric patterns suggest growing attention to workflow analysis, computer vision, surgical phase recognition, and newer model architectures. Further multicenter validation and prospective clinical evaluation are needed to determine whether these developments translate into generalizable and clinically meaningful applications.

title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
desc: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

title: Machine Learning Applications in Prostate Cancer Genomics: From Mutation Signatures to Clinical Prediction Models.
source: PubMed · Research and reports in urology
desc: [Research and reports in urology] Prostate cancer (PCa) is a highly heterogeneous disease with variable clinical outcomes. Advances in next-generation sequencing have enabled comprehensive genomic profiling, generating large-scale datasets that require sophisticated analytical tools. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful approach for extracting clinically relevant insights from these datasets. This narrative review examines current ML applications in PCa genomics, focusing on mutation signature analysis, biomarker discovery, and clinical prediction models. We also discuss the integration of genomic and clinical data, the limitations of current approaches, and how ML-driven methods can be translated into clinical practice.

title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
desc: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

title: Symmetry-Consistent Attention Supervision for Explainable Multi-label Temporal-Bone CT Assessment.
source: PubMed · Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
desc: [Journal of imaging informatics in medicine] The purpose of this study is to develop an explainable deep learning framework for region-wise, multi-label assessment of inner- and middle-ear status on temporal-bone computed tomography (CT). The framework used a ResNet-18 encoder with class-specific attention pooling to predict eight labels representing normal and congenital malformation states of the left and right inner and middle ears. Sparse polygon annotations supervised attention using masked binary cross-entropy, Dice-overlap, and outside-mask penalties. A left-right equivariant consistency regularizer enforced bilateral symmetry under horizontal flipping. The dataset comprised 2399 axial and coronal CT images from 87 patients. Development used fourfold patient-level cross-validation on 35 patients (1018 images), followed by evaluation on a held-out internal test set of 52 patients (1381 images). In cross-validation, the full model achieved a macro-AUC of 0.765 and a macro-F1 of 0.627. On the held-out internal test set, image-level evaluation yielded a macro-AUC of 0.688 and a macro-F1 of 0.572, representing the highest mean performance among the evaluated CNN, vision transformer, and MedViT baselines. Patient-level aggregation further yielded a macro-AUC of 0.716 and a macro-F1 of 0.621. The proposed attention maps were also more side-specific and anatomically concentrated than baseline heatmaps. Attention supervision and bilateral equivariance may improve interpretable temporal-bone CT assessment. Larger external studies and patient-level evaluation are required before clinical deployment.

title: CLADE: Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
desc: Retrieval-augmented systems often retrieve passages that are accurate and relevant but state the answer at a coarser level of granularity than the question requires. For example, a question may ask which specific disease a drug treats (familial hyperlipidemia), while the retrieved passage mentions the broader disease family (hyperlipidemia). Prior work on context sufficiency treats such coarse passages simply as insufficient. We argue that they form a distinct case, which we call resolvable insufficiency: text alone cannot settle the fine-grained answer, but the broader category it mentions maps to a short list of candidate answers in a domain ontology. When language models read these coarse, family-only passages, they exhibit a phenomenon we call Clade (Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence): they answer instead of abstaining or searching further. On biomedical questions from PrimeKG, family-only passages reduce abstention by 13.8 points compared to uninformative passages, and the resulting guesses are wrong about half the time. A counterfactual test confirms the cause: replacing an exact disease name with its broader family name lowers abstention by 17.4 points compared to deleting the sentence. Simple fixes like confidence filtering, scaling to a larger model, and explicitly instructing the model to abstain cannot resolve Clade, and this replicates on ecological species interactions in GloBI. Finally, we test whether an ontology can turn coarse passages into exact answers. Given the correct family, an ontology list includes the true answer in 98.5% of cases, but string matching finds that family on the page for only 19.8%. Letting the model choose the family raises this to 30.0% and end-to-end recovery from 10.0% to 26.8%. Overall, our results show when language models should stop guessing and consult an ontology, and highlight which steps of that process remain unsolved.

title: Prior-informed machine learning for clinically interpretable medical diagnosis.
source: PubMed · Frontiers in bioengineering and biotechnology
desc: [Frontiers in bioengineering and biotechnology] Traditional machine learning (ML) in medical diagnostics often suffers from limited clinical interpretability and poor generalization, owing to its black-box, data-driven nature. Here, we present Prior-Informed Machine Learning (PIML), a framework that integrates clinically grounded generative reasoning with data-driven, ML-enabled discriminative modeling through Bayesian inference to provide clinically interpretable, patient-specific diagnostic outcomes. By embedding the optimization of sensitivity and specificity in data-driven diagnosis-requirements for subsequent Bayesian inference-directly into the ML model development process, PIML enables a synergistic integration of machine learning and clinical expertise that cannot be achieved through either data-driven or clinically grounded approaches alone. PIML was validated across three clinical domains-cervical neoplasia detection, high-risk oral lesion detection, and preterm birth detection-where Bayesian inference was systematically employed to integrate electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)-based machine learning with domain-specific clinical expertise, thereby enabling more comprehensive and enhanced diagnostic decision-making. Our results demonstrate that PIML generally improves diagnostic performance compared with standard ML approaches and provides competitive or superior performance relative to knowledge-based and feature-level prior integration strategies. This work presents an innovative, systematic framework with strong potential for widespread adoption in addressing medical diagnostic challenges across heterogeneous clinical environments.

title: HandsOnAid: Building and Evaluating an Offline First-Aid Assistant for Emergency Response Scenarios
desc: Emergencies can occur where there is no phone signal and no ambulance nearby. A small language model on a phone can be helpful in such situations, but its advice needs to be safe and accurate. We built HandsOnAid, a 4-bit Gemma 2B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on FirstAidQA dataset, a corpus of 5,550 first-aid question-answer pairs. We compared seven configurations, including the base, 4-bit and 8-bit fine-tuned models, and versions with a length floor, safety gate, or retrieval. We used a 41-pair question-answer bank with medically reviewed references that followed ANZCOR guidelines, and a strict 0-5 score rubric, with twelve safety overrides. Four frontier LLM judges (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM-5.3) blindly scored every answer, with 45 hidden controls used to check judge reliability. Fine-tuning improved the mean score by +1.08 over the base model to 2.34. The best configuration scored 2.51 out of 5 which was the fine-tuned 4-bit model with retrieval. A medical professional also conducted a blind evaluation of 40 answers across the base, the 4-bit fine-tuned, and the retrieval configurations, and the scores were similar to the LLM judges' average scores. A keyword audit found limited coverage of several details of ANZCOR guidelines in the training corpus, that are required by the rubric, which suggests that missing information in the training data could be a cause of the low scores. On a smartphone device (Pixel 7 Pro) with six CPU threads and no network connection, the 4-bit fine-tuned model produced its first displayable text in 6.86 seconds and a complete answer in 14.88 seconds on average over ten questions.

title: Medical Artificial Intelligence for Rural Areas of Developing Countries a Boon or Bane: A Contemporary Narrative Review.
desc: [Health science reports] The integration of medical artificial intelligence (AI) in rural India holds transformative potential for enhancing healthcare access and quality. This narrative review examines the promising applications of medical AI in addressing healthcare disparities, increasing service efficiency, and mitigating physician shortages in underserved areas. However, challenges persist, including medical students' limited awareness and education about AI, reluctance to engage in rural health services, and migration trends affecting healthcare delivery. Effective implementation demands a multifaceted approach, tackling technological, economic, and contextual obstacles through stakeholder collaboration. Ethical considerations such as bias, data privacy, and local workforce involvement are paramount for the responsible deployment of medical AI. This review delves into both the opportunities and challenges, emphasizing the importance of addressing these issues through enhanced education and ethical frameworks. Ultimately, a balanced strategy is essential to harness the potential of medical AI in revolutionizing rural healthcare, highlighting the need for innovative policies that align technological advancements with community needs.

title: MEOW: Medical Open-World Interactive Segmentation
desc: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.

title: peleke-1: A Suite of Protein Language Models Fine-Tuned for Targeted Antibody Sequence Generation.
desc: [Viral immunology] The discovery of therapeutic antibodies is a traditionally arduous process. Today, the lab-based process of antibody discovery consists of several time-consuming steps that involve live animal immunization, B-cell harvesting, hybridoma creation, and then downstream engineering and evaluation. However, the use of artificial intelligence in drug design has previously been shown effective in the rapid generation of protein-specific binders, small molecules, and even antibody therapeutics, thereby replacing some of the primary steps of the drug discovery process. Here, we present peleke-1, a suite of protein language models fine-tuned from state-of-the-art large language models using curated antibody-antigen complex data. These models generate targeted antibody Fv sequences for a given antigen sequence input at-scale. This suite of models provides a reliable, artificial intelligence-driven approach for in silico therapeutic antibody discovery along with an open-source framework for future antibody language model tuning.

title: MicroBT: Centroid-Guided Synergistic Learning for Multi-Modal Micro Brain Tumor Segmentation and Counting
desc: Multi-modal brain tumor segmentation is essential for clinical diagnosis, radiotherapy planning, and longitudinal monitoring. While recent studies have achieved remarkable overall segmentation performance, they rely on overlap-based objectives that inherently favor large regions, causing sub-3 mm micro-lesions to be systematically suppressed during training. Moreover, existing pixel-level segmentation frameworks lack explicit instance-level modeling, leading to unreliable lesion counting that directly impacts clinical staging and therapeutic decisions. To address these challenges, we propose MicroBT, a unified multi-modal framework for micro brain tumor segmentation and counting. Our core insight is that a fundamental geometric property is inherently scale-invariant: regardless of size, each lesion possesses a well-defined centroid. Leveraging this, we first devise a centroid-anchored synergistic paradigm that utilizes predicted centroids as shared anchors to simultaneously condition dense segmentation and instance-level localization. To counteract the tumor size imbalance, we further devise a Volume-Calibrated Loss (VC-Loss) that adaptively amplifies the gradient contribution of micro-lesions, alongside a Size-Aware Curriculum Optimization (SACO) that stabilizes multi-task training by establishing global representations before progressively unlocking fine-grained localization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MicroBT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly on metastases, where micro-lesion ($\leq 3$ mm) localization precision improves by approximately 7% and counting estimation errors decrease by approximately 26%. The code is available at https://github.com/leonlou921/MicroBT.

title: A theory of multilevel interactive equilibrium in neuroAI.
source: PubMed · Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society
desc: [Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society] We propose a class of game-theoretic framework for adaptive multi-agent intelligent systems. Unlike the classical game theory which assumes that strategies are primitive objects chosen by perfectly rational agents, the new framework provides a mathematical foundation for studying equilibrium in NeuroAI and can be viewed as an extension of game theory with relaxed assumptions such as various degrees of uncertainty. At its core, Multilevel Interactive Equilibrium (MIE) generalizes the classical Nash equilibrium to intelligent systems with internal computation. Rather than being defined solely at the level of observable behavior, equilibrium emerges when neural learning dynamics, cognitive representations, and behavioral strategies mutually stabilize between interacting agents. This framework applies uniformly to interactions between two biological brains, two artificial agents, or hybrid human-AI systems. We discuss the emerging applications of multilevel game theory for human-autonomous vehicle driving, human-machine interactions, human-large language model (LLM) interactions, and computational psychiatry. We use simple computer simulations to provide proof-of-concept validation of MIE. We also outline experimental strategies and computational methods to estimate MIE and discuss challenges and prospects in future research.

title: The BRIDGE dataset: paired brightfield whole-slide images of prostate core-needle biopsies in paraffin, after deparaffinization and H&E staining
desc: Computational approaches are increasingly being explored to streamline histopathology workflows, including label-free methods that aim to reduce reliance on chemical staining. Among these, deep learning-based label-free virtual staining uses images of unstained tissue to computationally generate stained images. Despite growing interest, model development and validation remain constrained by the scarcity of paired, clinically annotated whole-slide imaging datasets. We present BRIDGE, a dataset of prostate core-needle biopsies collected at the Prof. Franciszek Lukaszczyk Oncology Centre in Bydgoszcz, Poland. The dataset comprises 869 glass slides from 169 patients, each digitized sequentially after sectioning, deparaffinization, and hematoxylin and eosin staining, yielding in total 2607 whole-slide images. The dataset supports the development and external validation of label-free virtual staining, virtual unstaining, image-registration and segmentation methods. Each slide is accompanied by a Gleason score, enabling downstream analyses of cancer classification and grading concordance. The stained images can be used independently for color normalization and cross-scanner robustness studies. All images are de-identified, distributed in their native scanner format and will be available through the BioImage Archive.

title: Dermatologist or AI? Patient Preferences in Skin Assessment.
desc: [Dermatology and therapy] Artificial intelligence (AI) is playing an expanding role in dermatology, particularly in diagnosing skin cancer and other cutaneous diseases. However, little is known about public perceptions towards AI for skincare evaluation and management. The purpose of this study was to assess public trust, comfort, and security concerns about AI-based facial evaluation. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 147 participants through Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) and REDCap. Participants rated comfort, trust, and security concerns regarding AI and dermatologist evaluation of facial images using a 5-point Likert scale. Wilcoxon Signed-Rank tests were used to compare preference for AI vs. dermatologists. Participants expressed greater confidence in dermatologists than AI for independent evaluation of facial features (mean 4.37 vs. 3.82, P < 0.001) and trust in creating a skincare management plan (mean 4.46 vs. 3.87, P < 0.001). Privacy and security concerns were prevalent, with 69% agreeing they were worried about security risks of AI facial imaging. Participants had confidence in AI technology for skincare evaluation and management, although they tended to prefer dermatologists over AI. Security was a concern for AI facial imaging.

title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models
desc: Benchmark scores for medical large language models (LLMs) are difficult to interpret when scoring criteria cannot be traced to clinical evidence. Here we developed Med Evidence Bench (MEB; https://www.medevidencebench.org.cn/), comprising 1,536 physician-constructed items across three levels: guideline knowledge, standardized clinical scenarios and real-world laboratory scenarios. Each criterion stating a medical claim is linked to a versioned source-text span. Across ten LLMs, the Evidence Trace Score (ETS) was 0.975-0.997 for guideline knowledge, 0.292-0.658 for standardized scenarios and 0.182-0.447 for real-world scenarios, and rankings varied across levels. For real-world scenarios, scores for identifying clinical information (mean, 0.770) exceeded those for matching evidence (0.165) or formulating recommendations (0.160). On 1,296 criterion-level judgments, automated grading agreed with the majority vote of three physicians (macro-F1, 0.930; 95% confidence interval, 0.915-0.945), although agreement was lower for evidence application. These findings from Chinese-language materials indicate that guideline recall does not ensure patient-specific evidence use and do not establish clinical effectiveness.

title: Ethical decision-making for large language model use: a six-step model for mental health professionals.
desc: [Frontiers in psychology] This article presents a six-step ethical decision-making model for mental health professionals confronted with ethical concerns arising when clients use large language models (LLMs) for mental health support. LLMs may introduce ethical problems that existing decision-making models were not designed to address. To provide guidance, we synthesized two bodies of research, the first concerning ethical risks posed by LLM use, and the second about existing decision-making models, to create a new model designed specifically for LLM and AI-related ethical issues. Our model addresses AI-specific phenomena such as deceptive empathy, algorithmic bias, digital attachment, and diffuse accountability structures. We propose this model as a conceptual foundation and encourage its ongoing refinement as AI continues to evolve.

title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
desc: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

title: Therapeutic Robots: Understanding the Limits of AI.
desc: [American journal of psychoanalysis] This paper critically examines the use of therapeutic chatbots based on artificial intelligence from a psychoanalytic perspective. Drawing on current literature, it questions the legitimacy of labeling these tools as "therapeutic," arguing that they lack essential elements such as subjectivity, transference, symbolization, and the capacity for psychic transformation. A case example illustrates how the relationship users establish with chatbots is narcissistic remaining in the "as if" register in the absence of a real other to enable intersubjectivity. Ethical, epistemological, and clinical implications are discussed, especially in relation to vulnerable populations. The paper highlights the urgency for ethical reflection, regulation, and long-term research as these technologies advance in the field of mental health.

title: What Factors Matter for Collection-Level Counting with Human-AI Collaboration?
desc: Many scientific and policy decisions require estimating the total number of target objects across a large image collection. Exhaustive human labeling is often infeasible, while raw model predictions can be biased, especially under domain shift. Recent human-AI estimation methods combine imperfect model predictions with limited human verification to obtain reliable collection-level estimates. However, existing work provides little guidance on how practitioners should choose among models, estimators, and adaptation strategies for a new deployment. We study these choices within a common human-in-the-loop counting framework across 12 tasks spanning biomedical microscopy, ground-level and aerial wildlife surveys, and overhead imagery of urban structures. Our results show that modern multimodal models provide a strong, training-free starting point for many tasks, while fine-tuned detectors become more advantageous at larger labeling budgets and across repeated deployments. Estimation efficiency improves further when model predictions are used to prioritize which units humans label, rather than sampling uniformly. We also find that each model's ranking quality can be estimated with a small pilot set, yielding practical guidance for selecting strategies on new counting tasks. In a field deployment on aerial pronghorn surveys, a task-specific adaptation of these methods meets the survey's $\pm 5\%$ tolerance after reviewing a median of only $3.2\%$ of collected images.

title: Artificial intelligence for automated lung nodule detection in chest computed tomography scans.
desc: [Breathe (Sheffield, England)] Automated detection of pulmonary nodules on computed tomography has evolved from rule-based image processing algorithms to sophisticated artificial intelligence (AI) systems capable of nodule localisation, volumetric measurement and malignancy risk stratification. Four landmark papers published between 1994 and 1999 established the computational foundations of this field, introducing grey-level thresholding, morphological feature extraction, neural networks and three-dimensional analysis as core detection principles. We provide an overview of these foundational studies and trace the subsequent evolution of AI-based nodule detection, from early computer-aided detection systems to modern deep learning frameworks evaluated in the context of lung cancer screening programmes.

title: Interleaving anatomical inspection and diagnostic reasoning for explainable radiology report generation
desc: Automated radiology report generation can draft clinically plausible reports, yet the pathway from visual evidence to reported findings remains opaque, leaving the diagnostic basis of these reports unexplained and the generated reports difficult to review or revise. We introduce ARIVE (Anatomy-guided Reasoning with Interleaved Visual Evidence), an explainable report generation framework that interleaves anatomical inspection with diagnostic reasoning prior to final report composition. To support this process, we constructed 159,416 multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) trajectories from MIMIC-CXR, wherein visual evidence from inspected anatomical regions informs subsequent clinical interpretation. Trained on these trajectories and further optimized using anatomical and clinical-content rewards, ARIVE achieved superior clinical-efficacy performance compared with strong baselines on MIMIC-CXR and the abnormality-centered MIMIC-ABN. ARIVE's reports were competitive with those of leading models in blinded expert grading, and its MCoT trajectories earned high ratings for diagnostic traceability. Furthermore, a paired review evaluation suggests that access to MCoT can aid in identifying errors within generated reports.

title: A large language model-based autonomous agent for scanning tunnelling microscopy.
desc: [Chemical science] Scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) provides real space access to molecular and atomic structures, but autonomous operation remains constrained by the need for expert decisions in parameter optimization, image assessment, data interpretation and probe recovery. Most autonomous scanning probe microscopy systems remain model-centric and task-specific, relying on labelled training data, fixed output classes, predefined reward functions or specific protocols. Here, we introduce STMClaw, an LLM-based autonomous STM agent implemented as a modular workflow. It coordinates autonomous STM experiments by integrating natural language instructions, instrument feedback, and retrieved domain knowledge, without requiring additional task-specific model training. The agent comprises modules for trajectory planning, image evaluation, probe conditioning, and molecular assignment based on literature. In an autonomous run, STMClaw generated 606 records, 554 positions were scanned and evaluated by the LLM and 52 candidate positions were skipped. The evaluator achieved F1 scores of 0.86 and 0.90 for the good and bad image classes using 13 reference examples per class, respectively. It also enabled the recovery of molecularly resolved images after probe degradation and linked STM images to evidence retrieved from the literature. These results support the feasibility of an LLM-based autonomous STM agent for adaptive, knowledge-aware surface science experimentation.

title: A Stage-Wise Explainable Pipeline for Arteriolar-to-Venular Ratio Estimation and Retinopathy Screening
desc: The arteriolar-to-venular diameter ratio (AVR) is a clinically motivated marker of retinal vascular health. We present a five-stage pipeline for AVR estimation and exploratory retinopathy screening from fundus images, with inspectable intermediate outputs at each stage. The pipeline combines vessel and artery-vein masks, optic-disc localization, vessel-calibre estimation using a minimal-chord boundary walk, and AVR computation from dominant arterial and venular branches. An explicit threshold-based rule produces the screening decision, enabling errors to be traced to individual processing stages. On an exploratory cohort of 30 HRF images, we report 96.7% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.968 and ROC-AUC of 0.978. Ablation studies and an exploratory comparison with VascX examine the effects of vessel pairing, calibre measurement and aggregation. Interpretation is limited by the small cohort, proxy disease labels and absence of independent reference calibre measurements. The pipeline provides a transparent framework for investigating retinal vascular biomarkers, with further validation needed on larger, clinically graded cohorts.

title: From Reactive to Proactive Care: How AI Is Connecting Rio's Residents to Public Services.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] In the sprawling city of Rio de Janeiro, accessing health care can be challenging, even when services are available. A new initiative aims to change that by using AI to proactively connect people to public services. In this News and Perspectives article, JMIR Correspondent Luke Taylor reports on the Connect Rio program, the second story in his two-part series on how AI is helping make health care more proactive in Brazil.

title: FedVP: Federated Learning across Heterogeneous Models by Pooling Locally Trained Verifiers
desc: Conventional federated learning relies on the shared model backbone to aggregate client updates, limiting collaboration among institutions that deploy large language models (LLMs) from different families and at different scales. We propose Federated Verifier Pool (FEDVP), a new federated learning paradigm that enables heterogeneous clients to collaborate through shared verification rather than parameter aggregation. Each client trains a verifier using local data and responses generated by its chosen LLM backbone. The server pools these independently trained verifiers and combines their judgments to select answers without merging model parameters. This allows both LLM backbones and verifiers to differ in architecture and size, while keeping the LLM backbones frozen and deriving collaborative gains from improved answer selection. We evaluate FEDVP across five public medical question-answering datasets treated as federated clients, using Qwen and LLaMA backbones ranging from 3B to 14B parameters. FEDVP consistently improves performance across all five clients and outperforms the strongest conventional federated baselines by 1.46-5.79 percentage points in mean accuracy.

title: The sociology of artificial intelligence development and utilisation in Africa.
desc: [Frontiers in sociology] Artificial Intelligence (AI) is impacting societies' social relations, institutions and social structures in definitive ways. Not many innovations have impacted human behaviours as significantly as AI. Deviating from the previous studies on AI that focuses on the potential implications of AI for everyday human society, this paper adopted secondary method of data collection, decolonial theory, and case study analysis to examine the sociological utilisation of AI in Africa. It provided answers to the fundamental sociological question of-why sociology of AI is needed in Africa? What forms of historical and social context shape AI's incursion into Africa? Findings from this study revealed that while AI in Africa is driving positive innovations like financial inclusion, climate resilience, agriculture and food security, rapid diagnosis, education and language inclusion and job creation, it is also exacerbating technological asymmetry, expanding existing inequalities, strengthening unequal geopolitical power relations and perpetuating historical institutional dynamics on the continent.

title: SepsisFlow: an event-stream foundation model for continuous risk warning and trajectory modelling in ICU sepsis
desc: Sepsis is a leading cause of ICU death with heterogeneous onset and course, yet most warning models predict only whether sepsis will occur, leaving clinicians uncertain of its onset context and early trajectory once an alarm sounds. To answer these questions on one hourly clock from ICU admission, we built SepsisFlow: before onset, it combines a Mamba model pretrained on 2.57 million EHRs with about 1,700 hourly features in gradient-boosted trees to predict 6/12/24-h risk; at onset, it fuses Mamba and tabular encoders via a gated network into continuous patient states defining onset contexts; after onset, it encodes 72-h organ-support and physiological trajectories via an attention bidirectional recurrent network into early courses. For pre-onset warning in MIMIC-IV, SepsisFlow detected more cases than NEWS2, qSOFA, and SIRS at equal alarms, gaining about 8 cases per 100 from hourly updating, while outperforming 16 retrained algorithms and maintaining risk ranking in eICU. At onset, its contexts separated 2% cardiovascular-ICU from 15%-17% other 28-day mortality, and within each context after onset, persistent support carried fivefold higher mortality than de-escalation. SepsisFlow establishes a foundation-model paradigm for continuous risk and trajectory stratification in critical care.

title: Deep Learning-Enhanced Lateral-Flow Microarray Biosensor for Multiplexed Inflammatory Biomarker Analysis.
desc: [Analytical chemistry] Beyond simply functional integration, achieving synergistic enhancements in multiplex detection, quantitative robustness, and intelligent analysis remains a key challenge for next-generation biosensing platforms in precision diagnostics. Lateral flow biosensors are attractive paper-based platforms because of their simplicity, low cost, and rapid operation; however, conventional line-type formats and visual readouts may limit their multiplex quantitative capability. Here, we present a surface-enhanced Raman scattering-based lateral flow microarray chip (LF-SERS-MAC) platform that integrates spatially encoded microarray patterns with AI-assisted analysis to enable sensitive, specific, and stable detection of three inflammatory proteins on a single paper device. The platform employs AuNPDTNB@antibody nanoprobes that simultaneously provide strong Raman signals and specific recognition of target proteins. The 4 × 4 microarray architecture enables spatially separated detection channels and predefined replicate microdots, supporting standardized SERS sampling and replicate-based signal averaging. More importantly, a 2D transformation-based deep learning model was developed for inflammation classification and concentration prediction, which demonstrates higher accuracy than conventional AI models. This platform can be further scaled to high-throughput paper chips, facilitating its clinical translation as a next-generation multiplexed intelligent biosensing strategy.

title: Predicting Single-Cell Spatial Gene Expression from H&E using Pathology Foundation Models
desc: Predicting gene expression directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images offers a scalable and cost-effective approach to deriving spatial molecular insights from routine histology. Pathology foundation models, typically pretrained using tile-level objectives, may not adequately capture the fine-grained cellular features required for single-cell molecular prediction. In this work, we systematically evaluate and establish domain-informed and task-specific strategies for adapting pathology foundation models to single-cell spatial gene expression prediction. Using paired H&E and Xenium 5K data, our approach improves mean gene-wise Pearson correlation by 2.67x over the standard zero-shot baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance on this task. We demonstrate strong gene-detection performance across the full gene panel (AUROC = 0.800) and importantly identify that predictive performance varies substantially across biological contexts, with our model achieving its highest Pearson correlation for spatially variable genes (r = 0.643). Our findings demonstrate that, despite the challenges of sparse single-cell measurements, H&E-derived representations can recover biologically meaningful spatial expression patterns, highlighting both the opportunities and limitations of morphology-based molecular inference at cellular resolution.

title: Did you cite your sources? Why bibliography matters.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] The burgeoning artificial intelligence ecosystem has changed every facet of the landscape of medical research, including the dissemination of results by writing and publishing research papers. The presence of hallucinated (fabricated, inaccurate, or incomplete) references in your bibliography calls into question the basis and validity of your work. In this Perspective, we reiterate the imperative of properly curating the reference list to support each standard section of a research article.

title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery
desc: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.

title: Rethinking Peer Review in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Tiered Model for Health Promotion Journals.
source: PubMed · American journal of health promotion : AJHP
desc: [American journal of health promotion : AJHP] The number of papers published in health promotion journals has grown substantially for two decades, and mainstream use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated that growth. Yet peer review remains fundamentally unchanged. Review still depends on volunteer time, and many journals prohibit reviewers from using AI to protect confidential, unpublished work. The result is an asymmetry: authors write faster with AI, while reviewers face mounting demand without the same tools. Funding agencies have begun responding; the NIH, for example, now caps annual application submissions per principal investigator. Journals cannot impose comparable limits because submissions are scattered across thousands of independent outlets, and requiring authors to complete reviews in proportion to their publications would be nearly impossible to enforce. We propose a solution that concentrates limited reviewer capacity on the most complex and consequential research. Cross-sectional and other descriptive studies would be evaluated by a purpose-built AI reviewer, trained to assess methodological rigor in such studies and designed not to retain or learn from unpublished manuscripts. Accepted papers would appear in a companion journal or section of the parent title. Traditional peer review would then be reserved for longitudinal, experimental, and other higher-impact research. Beyond easing reviewer burden, this model creates a transparent signal of rigor that could help tenure and promotion committees reward quality over publication quantity.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
desc: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

title: Drug Design and Discovery: The Long Road From Hansch Analysis to Artificial Intelligence.
desc: [ChemMedChem] The present article traces the long journey of the historical evolution and transformation of QSAR from its early days to its current role in drug discovery. It begins with the breakthrough created by the introduction of data analysis and highlights the major advances achieved throughout its development. Changes in molecular representation resulted in an explosion of molecular descriptors, while the rapid accumulation of large amounts of data demanded the application of elaborated statistical techniques. Today, machine learning and artificial intelligence have become integral components of pharmaceutical research, supporting every stage of the drug discovery pipeline, from target identification and hit discovery to lead optimization and the prediction of ADMET properties. At the same time, strict prerequisites have been established to ensure the development of QSAR models capable of reliable and robust predictions. Model validation, applicability domain, and model interpretability are fundamental principles of robust QSAR modeling. These principles are closely related to the distinction between local and global models, reflecting the trade-off between predictive performance, generalizability, and mechanistic interpretability. Finally, multi-objective optimization is discussed, as an approach to address the complex and often conflicting requirements, associated with successful drug candidates and decision-making throughout the drug discovery pipeline, including library design.

title: Deep Learning-Enabled Plasmonic-Catalytic Au@PBA Array for Simultaneous SERS/Colorimetric Quantification of Exhaled Benzene-Related VOCs.
desc: [Analytical chemistry] Accurate determination of benzene-related volatile organic compounds (B-VOCs) in exhaled breath is of considerable importance for disease screening and occupational exposure assessment. However, the simultaneous identification and quantification of structurally similar B-VOCs remain a challenge due to severe cross-interference and nonlinear signal coupling in multicomponent matrices. Herein, we report a deep learning-enabled plasmonic-catalytic sensor array based on core-shell Au@PBA(M) (M = Co, Ni, Mn) nanozymes featuring an ultrathin PBA shell for the multiplexed analysis of five B-VOCs (toluene, ethylbenzene, xylene, styrene, and phenol). The dual-response core-shell Au@PBA nanoparticles provide both strong plasmonic enhancement and peroxidase-mimicking activity, enabling the catalytic oxidation of TMB with concurrent surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) and colorimetric readouts. In the presence of different B-VOCs, the oxidation process is inhibited to different extents due to the differential binding affinities of the B-VOCs to the Au@PBA nanoparticles, generating highly characteristic dual-mode fingerprints. Based on this mechanism, linear discriminant analysis enabled reliable discrimination of the five B-VOCs. Notably, quantitative analysis of single-component systems demonstrated broad quantitative ranges of 0.001-500 ppm for ethylbenzene and phenol and 0.005-500 ppm for toluene, xylene, and styrene. More importantly, the integration of multichannel SERS fingerprints with an artificial neural network enabled simultaneous quantification of five B-VOCs in 25 complex breath-relevant samples, yielding excellent predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.97) and low root-mean-square errors (0.27-0.30 in log10 scale). These results demonstrate that the proposed strategy effectively resolves the cross-responsiveness of complex gas mixtures, providing a robust and noninvasive platform for intelligent breath analysis and environmental monitoring.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Visual Mapping of Viable and Necrotic Tissue During Wound Debridement: A Clinical Image Segmentation Study.
desc: [Annals of plastic surgery] Accurate distinction between viable and necrotic tissue is essential during wound debridement, but visual assessment may be affected by blood coverage, uneven illumination, blurred tissue transitions, and instrument occlusion. This study developed and evaluated a deep learning-assisted image segmentation method for wound tissue assessment. A retrospective data set of clinical wound debridement images was annotated at the pixel level as background, viable or preservable tissue, and necrotic or nonviable tissue. Tissue-aware copy-paste augmentation was used to improve necrotic tissue representation. A SegFormer-based semantic segmentation model with boundary-aware output was trained and evaluated using pixel accuracy, intersection over union (IoU), Dice coefficient, precision, recall, and boundary F1 score. The augmented data set contained 356 image-mask pairs, including 156 original and 200 synthesized pairs. Training, validation, and test sets included 249, 53, and 54 samples, respectively. On the test set, pixel accuracy was 98.01%. For viable and necrotic tissue, mean IoU and mean Dice were 85.97% and 92.45%, respectively. Dice scores were 92.24% for viable tissue and 92.67% for necrotic tissue. Necrotic tissue recall was 94.09%, and mean boundary F1 was 61.83%. The proposed method showed strong region-level agreement with expert annotations and high sensitivity for necrotic tissue. Color-coded prediction maps and overlay visualizations may support wound tissue assessment, although exact boundary localization remained less accurate. Larger independent clinical data sets are needed for further validation.

title: Voltage-Current-Emission Framework of Time-Resolved Electroluminescence.
desc: [Nano letters] Time-resolved electroluminescence has been a central methodology for the development of LED devices. However, it still lacks quantitative theoretical descriptions of time-resolved electroluminescence. By combining the equivalent circuit models of semiconductor devices and the carrier dynamics of electroluminescence processes, here we have developed a voltage-current-emission framework to illustrate time-resolved electroluminescence from the pulse voltage as input, to injection current, and finally generate electroluminescence as output. The features of different LED devices can be quantitatively interpreted, confirming their universal applicability across LEDs with different materials and device structures. Importantly, the curves of time-resolved electroluminescence can be simulated to quantitatively describe the dynamics of current and carriers of the LED operation. In all, the voltage-current-emission framework offers theoretical guidance for achieving advanced LED devices for artificial intelligence (AI) technology.

title: Deep learning-based identification and counting of early-stage follicles in rat ovaries.
desc: [Veterinary pathology] Counting ovarian early follicles helps assess the impact of pharmaceuticals and endocrine-disrupting chemicals on female fertility. Traditional manual counting methods are labor-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to intra- and interobserver variability, leading to inconsistent results. This study addresses these limitations by developing a fully automated solution for the identification and quantification of early-stage follicles in hematoxylin and eosin-stained rat ovarian sections, with the aim of enhancing efficiency, accuracy, and reproducibility. We developed a deep learning model designed to identify primordial type 1 and type 2 follicles, and a second model focusing on detecting early growing follicles. The automated system exhibited high performance on an independent test data set of 200 whole-slide images, whose predictions were validated by pathologists. The models achieved high precision and recall, with 98.49% and 90.92%, respectively, for type 1; 95.97% and 97.54% for type 2; and 99.45% and 80.09% for early growing follicles. Further comparisons with manual annotations performed by 4 independent pathologists revealed significant interobserver variability. While human performance was hindered by factors such as fatigue and inconsistent criteria application, resulting in variable precision and recall and high rates of missed follicles, the algorithm maintained superior consistency and overall higher F1-scores. Furthermore, a comparison between manual work and the algorithm's productivity showed that the algorithm was 11 times faster than manual quantification. These results demonstrate that the automated approach not only matches expert accuracy but also effectively eliminates subjectivity and diagnostic drift inherent in manual counting, providing a reproducible method for follicle counting, and significantly enhancing workflow efficiency.

title: Hierarchical supervised contrastive learning with AP-attention encoding for Wi-Fi fingerprinting indoor localization.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Indoor localization based on Wi-Fi fingerprinting has attracted significant research attention due to its infrastructure-free deployment and the ubiquitous availability of IEEE 802.11 access points (APs). A widely adopted deep learning architecture employs a stacked autoencoder (SAE) for unsupervised feature pre-training followed by a supervised multi-label classifier for hierarchical building, floor, and reference-point estimation. However, the SAE pre-training optimizes a mean squared error (MSE) reconstruction objective that is fundamentally misaligned with the downstream localization task, and it treats all 520 AP measurements uniformly despite many being uninformative at any given location. This study proposes HiSCL-AE, a two-component architectural modification: (1) an AP Importance Gate (AIG) that learns a per-AP sigmoid attention weight to adaptively suppress irrelevant APs end-to-end; and (2) a hierarchical supervised contrastive pre-training strategy (HiSCL) that replaces the MSE reconstruction objective with the supervised contrastive loss applied simultaneously at the building, floor, and reference-point granularities, directly optimizing the embedding geometry for localization. Experiments on the public UJIIndoorLoc benchmark demonstrate that HiSCL-AE achieves 90.73% building-floor accuracy and a mean positioning error of 11.38 m, outperforming the SAE baseline on both primary metrics (90.37% accuracy and 11.48 m error). Beyond accuracy, the AIG produces an interpretable AP importance map, revealing that fewer than 60 of 520 APs account for the majority of the discriminative signal-a finding with direct implications for radio map compression and network planning. We compared HiSCL-AE with six additional Wi-Fi fingerprinting methods under an identical experimental protocol; HiSCL-AE simultaneously achieves the highest Building+Floor accuracy and the lowest positioning error among the six methods compared.

title: Deep Learning Reconstruction for Accelerated Radial CEST MR Fingerprinting.
desc: [ArXiv] To accelerate chemical exchange saturation transfer magnetic resonance fingerprinting (CEST-MRF) using temporal deep learning reconstruction. Ten healthy volunteers underwent repeated test-retest golden-angle radial CEST-MRF acquisitions with 30 measurements and 34 spokes per measurement. The Movienet network was adapted to reconstruct accelerated radial CEST-MRF data. Separate models were trained using 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 20, and 34 spokes per measurement. Temporal and coil correlations were exploited by concatenating time and coil dimensions in the input. GRASP-based locally low-rank (GRASP-LLR) reconstruction was used for comparison. Quantitative DRONE fitting generated tissue parameter maps. Movienet-8 was evaluated with leave-one-subject-out analysis. Prospectively acquired 8-spoke datasets were compared with paired 34-spoke acquisitions, and Movienet-8 and Movienet-34 were compared with a 64-spoke acquisition. In the held-out retrospective series, median Pearson correlations between Movienet and GRASP-LLR were 0.795, 0.947, 0.974, 0.977, and 0.981 for 1, 8, 16, 20, and 34 spokes, respectively. Corresponding NRMSE values were 14.7, 8.2, 5.9, 5.3, and 5.1 percent. Across 10 leave-one-subject-out volunteers, median image correlation was 0.965 and NRMSE was 7.5 percent. Reconstruction of a 30-slice series required 1.7 s with Movienet versus approximately 45 min with GRASP-LLR. Movienet enables whole-brain radial CEST-MRF acquisition in 3 min, with image reconstruction in less than 2 s.
